items.prompt: Should pupils be allowed to bring mobile phones to school? Write a balanced argument with points for and against, and a conclusion.

criteria.label: The introduction states the question clearly
Gives points for and against, each with a reason or example
Uses linking phrases such as however, on the other hand and on balance
Uses a formal, impersonal style
The conclusion weighs up both sides and gives a view
Spelling, grammar and punctuation are accurate

planning: How will your introduction state the question?
What are two or three points for, with evidence or examples?
What are two or three points against, with evidence or examples?
Which side is stronger in your conclusion, and why?
items.model:
Should Pupils Bring Mobile Phones to School?

Many families now give their children mobile phones. Should pupils be allowed to bring them to school?

Supporters argue that phones help keep children safe, because parents can contact them on the way home. Phones can also be useful for learning, for example to record a science experiment.

On the other hand, phones can distract pupils during lessons. Some people also worry that expensive phones could be lost or damaged.

On balance, I believe pupils should be allowed to bring phones, as long as they are switched off and kept in a locker until the end of the day. This keeps the safety benefit without the distraction.
hints: Keep your own opinion until the conclusion.
Use a new paragraph for each side of the argument.
Phrases such as some people believe help you sound fair.
items.explanation: A balanced argument presents both sides fairly, with evidence, before giving a conclusion.

items.prompt: Write a formal letter to your town council asking for a pedestrian crossing near your school. Explain the problem and suggest a solution.

criteria.label: Uses formal letter layout with a suitable greeting and sign-off
Explains the problem clearly, with evidence
Makes a clear, polite request
Uses formal vocabulary and avoids contractions
Organises ideas into paragraphs
Spelling and punctuation are accurate

planning: What is the problem, and where exactly is it?
What evidence can you give, such as how busy the road is?
What exactly do you want the council to do?
How will you end politely and formally?
items.model:
Dear Sir or Madam,

I am writing on behalf of the pupils of SD Mekar Sari to request a pedestrian crossing on Jalan Diponegoro, outside our school gate.

Every morning, more than 300 pupils cross this road. During a survey last week, our class counted an average of 42 vehicles passing the gate every five minutes between 6.30 and 7.00. Many drivers do not slow down, and younger pupils often wait several minutes before it is safe to cross.

A zebra crossing with flashing lights would warn drivers and allow pupils to cross safely.

I would be grateful if the council could consider this request at its next meeting.

Yours faithfully,

Annisa Rahma, School Council
hints: Give real details: the name of the road, the time of day and what you have seen.
Remember: Dear Sir or Madam goes with Yours faithfully.
items.explanation: A formal letter of request explains a problem with evidence, makes a clear request and keeps a polite, formal tone.

items.prompt: Write an explanation of a natural process, such as the water cycle or how a seed grows. Use a title, subheadings and cause and effect connectives.

criteria.label: Has a title, an introduction and subheadings
Explains each stage in a logical order
Uses cause and effect connectives such as consequently and as a result
Uses and explains technical words
Uses the present tense and a formal style
Spelling and punctuation are accurate

planning: Which process will you explain, and what happens first?
Which subheadings will split the explanation into stages?
Which technical words will you use, and how will you explain them?
Which connectives will show cause and effect?
items.model:
How a Seed Becomes a Plant

A seed contains a tiny young plant and a store of food. With the right conditions, it grows into a new plant.

Waking up
When a seed takes in water, its coat softens and splits. This stage is called germination, and it also needs warmth and air.

Roots and shoots
First, a root grows downwards to anchor the seedling and take in water. Next, a shoot grows upwards towards the light.

Making food
Once the first leaves open, the plant makes its own food using light, water and carbon dioxide from the air. As a result, it no longer needs the food stored in the seed.
hints: Subheadings help the reader find each stage of the process.
Explain each technical word the first time you use it.
items.explanation: An explanation describes how or why something happens, stage by stage, using technical words and cause and effect connectives.

items.prompt: Write a biography of someone who has made a difference to their community, or of a famous Indonesian. Use paragraphs in time order.

criteria.label: Uses the third person and the past tense consistently
Events are in clear time order, with dates or time phrases
Each paragraph covers one stage of the person’s life
Includes specific facts and achievements
Ends by explaining why the person matters
Spelling, grammar and punctuation are accurate

planning: What are the key dates and events in the person’s life?
What problems did they face, and how did they deal with them?
What are they remembered for?
How will your last paragraph show why they matter today?
items.model:
Wati Susanti was born in 1975 in a small fishing village near Gresik. Her parents could not afford many books, so she read old newspapers that her father brought home from the market.

After finishing secondary school, she trained as a teacher in Surabaya. In 2001, she returned to her village and found that the children there had no library at all.

In 2003, she turned the front room of her house into a reading corner with forty donated books. Within ten years, it had grown into a community library with more than 5,000 books and weekly story sessions.

Today, her library still opens every afternoon, and several of the children who once read in her front room have become teachers themselves.
hints: Collect the key dates and events first, and put them in order.
Include at least one difficulty the person faced and how they dealt with it.
items.explanation: A biography tells the story of a real person’s life in time order, using facts, dates and the third person, and shows why the person matters.

items.prompt: Write a story that begins on the morning of a competition. Flash back to how the main character prepared, then return to the competition for the ending.

criteria.label: Opens with an engaging scene on the day of the competition
Uses a clear flashback, signalled with time phrases or had
Returns smoothly to the present for the ending
Shows feelings through actions, dialogue and figurative language
Uses paragraphs and punctuates dialogue correctly

planning: What is the competition, and how does your character feel that morning?
Which memory will your flashback show?
How will you signal the jump back and the return to the present?
What happens in the end, and what has your character learned?
items.model:
The starting pistol was in the referee’s hand, and Dani’s legs felt like jelly.

Three months earlier, he had stood on the same track, gasping, while the others finished a whole lap ahead. That night, Kakek had handed him a battered stopwatch. “Every morning before school,” he had said. “Just you and the clock.”

So every morning, while the street was still grey and quiet, Dani had run. Some days he had beaten the clock. Most days he had not.

Bang!

Dani flew. By the last bend, he could hear only his own breathing. He came third, but he crossed the line four seconds faster than ever before.

In the crowd, Kakek held up the stopwatch and grinned.
hints: Use a time phrase such as Three months earlier to start the flashback.
Use had in the flashback: he had trained, she had practised.
items.explanation: A flashback interrupts the main story to show an earlier event. It helps the reader understand why the present moment matters to the character.

items.prompt: Write a persuasive article for your school magazine arguing that every class should have one lesson a week outdoors. Use at least three persuasive techniques.

criteria.label: States a clear viewpoint at the start
Gives at least three reasons with evidence
Uses persuasive techniques such as rhetorical questions and emotive language
Answers an opposing view
Ends with a strong conclusion or call to action
Spelling, grammar and punctuation are accurate

planning: What is your main argument, in one sentence?
Which three reasons are strongest, and what evidence supports each one?
Which techniques will you use: rhetorical questions, facts, emotive words?
How will you answer people who disagree?
What will your final sentence be?
items.model:
Learning Under the Sky

How much of your school day do you spend looking at four walls? For most of us, the answer is almost all of it. It is time for every class to have one lesson a week outdoors.

First, outdoor lessons bring learning to life. Measuring the shadow of a tree teaches angles better than any diagram.

Secondly, after lessons outside, many pupils say they feel calmer and more ready to work.

Some teachers worry about rain or noise. However, our school has a covered terrace and a quiet garden that are empty most mornings.

One lesson a week costs nothing and needs no new equipment. Let us take our learning outside.
hints: Open with a question or a surprising fact to hook your reader.
Think about what a teacher might worry about, and answer that worry.
items.explanation: A persuasive article states a clear view, supports it with reasons and evidence, answers objections and ends with a call to action.

items.prompt: Which of these is a feature of a formal letter?

options.why: This is an informal way to end a message.
This is a heading in a recipe.

hints: Think about how a formal letter ends.
Formal letters use polite, set phrases.
Cross out the options that belong to stories, recipes and chats.
items.explanation: Yours faithfully is a formal sign-off, used when the letter begins Dear Sir or Madam.

items.prompt: Which sentence would best open a balanced argument?

options.text: Should pupils wear school uniform? There are strong views on both sides.
School uniform is the worst idea ever invented!
options.why: This is one-sided and informal, so it does not suit a balanced argument.

options.text: Once upon a time, a boy lost his school tie.
Buy your uniform at our shop today!

hints: A balanced argument looks at both sides of a question.
Its opening usually introduces the question without taking a side.
Find the opening that mentions both sides.
items.explanation: A balanced argument begins by introducing the question and showing that there are different views.

items.prompt: Put the parts of a news report in order.
items: Opening paragraph: who, what, where and when
hints: Think about the front page of a newspaper.
The most important information comes first, and details come later.
Start with the large words at the very top.
items.explanation: A news report starts with a headline and the reporter’s name. The opening paragraph gives the key facts, then come details and quotations, and the end looks ahead.

options.text: Mira walked onto the stage and began to dance.
options.why: This happens in the present of the story.

options.text: Tomorrow, Mira will dance on the stage.
options.why: This looks forward to the future.

options.text: As she waited on the stage, Mira remembered the day her grandmother had first taught her to dance.
Mira danced, and the audience clapped loudly.
options.why: This tells events in order, with no jump back.

hints: A flashback takes the reader back to an earlier time.
Look for words such as remembered and had.
Find the sentence that moves from the present to the past.
items.explanation: Remembered and had first taught take the reader back to an earlier event, so this sentence uses a flashback.
